new_statements.quote: [p.141] Minor syllables (or semi-, reduced, or pre-syllables) are similar to the Vʔ rhymes discussed above in that they are shorter and often offer fewer contrasts than major syllables. Such syllables do not occur on the final edge of a word and may be derived through shortening of syllables in weak prosodic positions; in these iambic languages that is the initial edge of a prosodic foot. [p.237] This split describes the difference between the first and second syllables of an iamb, as in the Zophei word pa hnaa ‘snore.’ Matisoff (1989) refers to this minor+major syllable iambic structure as a ‘sesquisyllable.’ More than one minor syllable may precede a major syllable, but minor syllables are never found on the final edge of a prosodic word or phrase.
new_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson Alexander. 2021. The Sound Systems of Zophei Dialects and Other Maraic Languages. PhD dissertation, Indiana University, Bloomington.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 5.2.6 'Minor syllables', printed p.141 (pdf p.159); Sec. 6.5, printed p.237 (pdf p.255); supporting: Sec. 4.7 p.128 (pdf 146), Sec. 6.5.1 pp.238-239 (pdf 256-257), Sec. 6.3.2 p.222 (pdf 240)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zophei is a tone language (Lawngtlang Zophei: underlying H vs L vs toneless on every syllable). Word prosody is iambic (sesquisyllabic): one or more reduced minor syllables (Ca, vowel only [ə], shorter, sometimes devoiced) occupy the weak initial position of the foot, and the full major syllable, the prosodically strong one, is always word/phrase-final; i.e. prominence sits on the final (major) syllable. No contrastive stress is described; prominence is a matter of foot structure, not a lexical stress feature.
new_statements.exceptions: Minor syllables in Lawngtlang Zophei, unlike Hakha Lai or Lemi, retain an L/M/H pitch contrast (pp.238-239, Fig. 6.9), and a major syllable shortened to a minor syllable keeps its tone (bèh + tsih -> bà tsih). Minor-syllable vowels may devoice/delete in some prosodic positions (sa tlee poo, p.128). CVʔ syllables reduced in non-final position are treated as minor syllables (p.241-242).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the prosodic foot / prosodic word or phrase (minor syllables barred from the final edge of a prosodic word or phrase); data are Lawngtlang and Tlawngrang Zophei elicited words and verbal complexes. The author explicitly notes (p.243/HL 2023) that in KC iambic structure it is often unclear whether tonal contour licensing targets the final edge or the prominent syllable, since they coincide.
new_statements.identity_note: Lotven 2021 describes three Zophei village varieties: Lawngtlang Zophei (LTZ, 'Lower Zophei B'), Tlawngrang Zophei (TRZ) and Nuitah/Leitak Zophei (NTZ), all under Zyphe [zyp], glottocode zyph1238 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes known to me). The tone analysis and the minor-syllable pitch data are LTZ; the iambic/minor-syllable statements are made for Zophei generally (examples from both TRZ and LTZ). The dissertation also sketches Zotung, Senthang, Mara and Lutuv second-hand; those passages were not used here.

Word prosody is described as iambic/sesquisyllabic: minor syllables (Ca [ə], reduced, 'non-word-final') precede the major syllable; 'in these iambic languages [the weak position] is the initial edge of a prosodic foot' (p.141); 'the first and second syllables of an iamb, as in the Zophei word pa hnaa' and 'minor syllables are never found on the final edge of a prosodic word or phrase' (p.237); minor syllables in Lawngtlang Zophei nonetheless keep an L/M/H pitch contrast (pp.238-2…

sources.note: Repeats the dissertation passage: minor+major 'iamb, as in the Zophei word pa hnaa "snore"'; sesquisyllable structure 'favors iambic feet, prosodically weak-strong' (p.44 and Sec. on attractors). Nothing further on Zophei stress.

sources.note: Family-level statement (p.15): 'In sesquisyllabic words, a stressed "major syllable" is preceded by a short, unstressed C or CV "minor syllable"... resulting in an iambic (unstressed-stressed) word structure'; p.22 'in these iambic languages, that position [of reduction] is the left edge of the prosodic word'; Zophei cited for vowel inventories and minor-syllable vowel devoicing (sa tleé poó), no Zophei-specific stress rule.
